config.title: Build fallback strategy for provider outages

intro.title: Build fallback strategy for provider outages
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a fallback strategy to handle outages from external service providers, ensuring your Node.js application remains resilient. You will learn to implement a simple circuit breaker pattern using conditional logic and error handling in JavaScript. The main constructs involved include try-catch blocks, HTTP requests with the 'node-fetch' module, and state management for tracking provider status. By the end, you'll have a function that automatically switches to a backup provider when the primary one fails, making your app more reliable for users.
intro.usecase: Fallback strategies for provider outages are essential in production systems that rely on third-party APIs like payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal), geolocation services (Google Maps, Mapbox), or email/SMS providers (SendGrid, Twilio). For example, an e-commerce checkout system might automatically switch to a backup payment processor when the primary gateway is down, ensuring customers can complete purchases during outages. Similarly, a weather dashboard might display cached data or use an alternative weather API when the main service is unavailable. Developers implement these strategies to maintain service reliability and prevent single points of failure in critical user-facing features.

objectives: Implement a primary provider function that simulates an API call
Construct a fallback provider function to handle primary provider failures
Configure a retry mechanism to attempt the primary provider before switching
Integrate a health check to monitor provider availability
Manipulate error handling to gracefully switch between providers
Initialize a provider selection strategy based on health status
Apply logging to track provider usage and fallback events

steps.title: Import required Node.js modules
steps.instruction: Import the built-in Node.js 'http' module and assign it to a constant named 'http'.
steps.hint: Use the CommonJS require() syntax to import the http module. For example: const moduleName = require('module-name');
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a built-in Node.js module
const fs = require('fs');
steps.expectedOutcome: The http module is imported and available for making HTTP requests in your application.
successCriteria: The http module is imported using require() and assigned to a constant named 'http'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct module name 'http' and assigning it to a constant named 'http'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The http module needs to be imported using require('http') and assigned to a constant. Check the syntax and try again.

steps.title: Define primary and fallback provider URLs
steps.instruction: Create two constants named PRIMARY_PROVIDER_URL and FALLBACK_PROVIDER_URL with example API endpoint URLs as strings.
steps.hint: Use const declarations with descriptive names. Choose realistic example URLs like 'https://api.primary-provider.com/data' and 'https://api.backup-provider.com/data'.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have two string constants representing your primary and backup API endpoints ready for use in the fallback strategy.
successCriteria: Constants PRIMARY_PROVIDER_URL and FALLBACK_PROVIDER_URL are defined with string values representing API endpoints.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You defined at least one provider URL, but remember to create both PRIMARY_PROVIDER_URL and FALLBACK_PROVIDER_URL constants.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constants weren't defined correctly. Make sure you create two const variables with the exact names PRIMARY_PROVIDER_URL and FALLBACK_PROVIDER_URL, each assigned a string URL value.

steps.title: Create the request function skeleton
steps.instruction: Create an async function named makeRequest that takes a URL parameter.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before function and include a parameter for the URL. The function body can be empty for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an async function named makeRequest that accepts a URL parameter.
successCriteria: The code contains an async function named makeRequest with a URL parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've created an async function named makeRequest that takes a URL parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create an async function named makeRequest with a URL parameter.

steps.title: Implement the HTTP request logic
steps.instruction: Inside the makeRequest function, implement the HTTP GET request logic using the http.get method wrapped in a Promise.
steps.hint: Use http.get(url, callback) where the callback handles the response. Remember to resolve the Promise with the response data or reject it with an error.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function should now contain a Promise that wraps an http.get call, handling response data collection and error events.
successCriteria: makeRequest returns a Promise that uses http.get with proper response handling (data collection and error handling).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started implementing the request logic, but check if you're properly handling the response data stream and error events.
steps.feedbackWrong: The implementation doesn't match the expected structure. Review how to use http.get within a Promise with proper response handling.

steps.title: Add error handling for individual requests
steps.instruction: Inside the makeRequest function, add a try-catch block around the HTTP request logic and check for non-200 HTTP status codes.
steps.hint: Wrap the request logic in try { ... } catch (error) { ... } and check if response.statusCode !== 200 inside the callback.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function will have basic error handling for network errors and HTTP status codes.
successCriteria: The makeRequest function contains a try-catch block and checks response.statusCode.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include both the try-catch block and the status code check.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function still needs error handling. Add a try-catch block and check the HTTP status code.

steps.title: Create the fallback strategy function
steps.instruction: Create an async function named fetchWithFallback that tries the primary provider first.
steps.hint: Define the function with the async keyword and use the primaryProvider constant as the first URL to try.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async function named fetchWithFallback that will contain the fallback logic.
successCriteria: An async function named fetchWithFallback is created and uses the primaryProvider constant.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've created an async function named fetchWithFallback that references the primaryProvider.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Create an async function named fetchWithFallback that will handle trying the primary provider first.

steps.title: Add fallback to secondary provider
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchWithFallback function, add a catch block after the try block that attempts to make a request to the fallbackProvider URL.
steps.hint: Use the same makeRequest function you created earlier to call the fallback provider when the primary request fails.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchWithFallback function should now have a catch block that attempts to call makeRequest with the fallbackProvider URL when the primary request fails.
successCriteria: The catch block contains a call to makeRequest with fallbackProvider as the argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a catch block, but make sure you're calling makeRequest with the fallbackProvider URL inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The catch block should contain a call to makeRequest with the fallbackProvider URL to implement the fallback strategy.

steps.title: Create the main execution function
steps.instruction: Create an async function named 'main' that will orchestrate the fallback strategy. The function should call fetchWithFallback and handle the result.
steps.hint: Define an async function called main. Inside it, use a try/catch block to call fetchWithFallback and log the result or any errors.
steps.expectedOutcome: An async function named 'main' is defined, which will serve as the entry point to execute the fallback strategy.
successCriteria: The code includes an async function named 'main' that contains a try/catch block and calls fetchWithFallback.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function is async and named 'main'. It should also include error handling with try/catch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create an async function named 'main' that calls fetchWithFallback and handles errors.

steps.title: Call the fallback strategy and handle results
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, call fetchWithFallback and log the successful response to the console.
steps.hint: Use await with fetchWithFallback to get the response, then log it with console.log.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will execute the fallback strategy and display the successful response in the console.
successCriteria: fetchWithFallback is called inside main with await, and the response is logged using console.log.
